title: As Trump’s Wall Closes in, DHS Intimidates a Border Tribe With Surveillance, Masked Agents and Drones
author: Ryan Devereaux
content:
At 4:59 a.m. on Aug. 25, Verlon Jose, the chairman of the Tohono O’odham
Nation in Southern Arizona, received an email from the head of the U.S. Border
Patrol’s Tucson Sector. Government contractors were en route to conduct soil
tests for construction of a 62-mile wall along the Nation’s southern boundary,
wrote acting chief patrol agent Henry N. Laxdal.

If the tribe wished to have cultural monitors observe the work, they were
welcome to, but they could not interfere with the government’s operations.

The work would begin in exactly one minute.

Jose, 59, was already aware of the contractors’ arrival. An hour earlier, a
tribal member had called to report a caravan heading south through the
reservation, and Facebook was lighting up with similar accounts. The convoy
included not only work trucks and drilling rigs, but Border Patrol vehicles as
well.

Dozens of border wall contractor and Border Patrol vehicles pass the Tadai
Me:i prayer camp on the morning of Aug. 27. Nate Sosa

For months, the O’odham had maneuvered to avoid such a scene, taking their
case to federal court. Their homeland straddles the border, and thousands of
tribal members live in Mexico. A wall would disrupt routine border crossings
for ceremonies and family visits and destroy landscapes they consider their
duty to protect, members and leaders say. Their lawsuit argued that the Trump
administration’s efforts to build it despite their opposition constituted an
historic attack on tribal sovereignty.

But administration attorneys gave assurances that the government was engaging
with the O’odham in good faith, and a judge in Washington, D.C., denied the
tribe’s request for a preliminary injunction. In his Aug. 25 email providing
Jose a 60-second heads up, the Border Patrol chief said his agency’s
willingness to accommodate cultural monitors underscored its “commitment to
ongoing coordination” with the Nation.

As daylight broke, Jose learned the contractors were guarded by federal agents
in masks and tactical gear, drawn from a special operations cadre that
participated in citywide sweeps in Minneapolis and Chicago the previous year,
which left three people dead, including two U.S. citizens. When the tribe’s
chief of police tried to reach the worksite, he was stopped at a roadblock set
up by the agents.

![Border Patrol agents in tactical gear stand near parked white and green
trucks in a desert landscape.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/D5612E06-F25D-4891-8753-A68B9ABB663C_d64c8e.jpg)Merrian
Felix ![A border patrol agent dressed in tactical gear sits in a tactical
vehicle in a desert landscape.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260826_091732_70f147.jpg)Davy Cross

Border Patrol tactical team members amass around the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on
Aug. 26.

Jose issued [a statement](https://www.tonation-nsn.gov/federal-agents-and-
contractors-enter-tohono-oodham-nation/) on the Nation’s website declaring the
incursion illegal and revealing that the Department of Homeland Security had
deployed a surveillance blimp and enlisted Mexican security forces to help
protect the work crews.

For a quarter-century, Tohono O’odham leaders have staved off a border wall by
allowing DHS to use the reservation as a testing ground for some of the
government’s most aggressive homeland security measures — from [vehicle
barriers](https://tolc-nsn.org/docs/Actions04/04095.pdf) on the reservation’s
southern boundary, to state-of-the-art [surveillance
towers](https://theintercept.com/2019/08/25/border-patrol-israel-elbit-
surveillance/), to law enforcement partnerships with the [Border
Patrol](https://tolc-nsn.org/docs/Actions16/16141.pdf) and [Immigration and
Customs Enforcement](https://www.ice.gov/hsi/our-partners/shadow-wolves).

Despite the collaborations, and assurances from the Trump administration,
ProPublica found that DHS has turned its vast apparatus on tribal members,
with 24-hour surveillance directed at an ongoing border prayer ceremony and
tribal members being questioned outside the reservation about their ceremonial
activities. ProPublica’s account is based on photos, videos, court filings,
interviews with tribal leadership, firsthand observations and more than 1,000
contemporaneously written observations compiled by tribal members.

The battle over a border wall on the Nation has broken along familiar partisan
lines in Arizona. While [GOP legislative
leaders](https://www.kjzz.org/politics/2026-07-13/arizona-lawmakers-back-dhs-
in-lawsuit-from-tohono-oodham-over-border-wall) have filed briefs in support
of the project, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs has [done the
same](https://tucson.com/news/local/border/article_f2815db6-3ac3-41aa-a096-f5486b5961b5.html)
in support of the tribe.

Progressive U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, whose district includes the
reservation, has said she is [crafting
legislation](https://news.azpm.org/s/103938-rep-grijalva-calls-on-federal-
government-to-stop-border-wall-construction-on-tribal-lands/) to rein in the
Department of Homeland Security’s sweeping powers to waive federal laws in
order to expedite wall construction. The Trump administration has used those
authorities to circumvent environmental and cultural preservation statutes on
[60 occasions](https://u.osu.edu/madsen.34/dhs-waivers/) across its two terms.

For Deshane Gregg, whose vehicle was forced off the road by a convoy of
contractors and federal agents, the recent show of force on the reservation
has felt like a government siege, not cooperation.

“You just feel helpless. You see these people, and they’re just so aggressive.
They want you to react. They want you to show them that we could be ugly too,”
she said. “We’re just here doing prayer. We’re just here, not trying to bother
them, but it gets to you when it’s constantly being like that.”

“The drones flying over us all day,” she added, “it’s a lot.”

A drone hovers over the Tadai Me:i camp during morning prayer songs on Aug.
27. Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica

ProPublica sent DHS, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and the Border Patrol
nearly 30 questions about the government’s surveillance and interactions with
tribal members and leaders. The agencies answered none of those questions.
Instead, CBP pointed to [a
statement](https://www.cbp.gov/newsroom/announcements/statement-cbp-
commissioner-rodney-s-scott-arizona-border-security-project) Commissioner
Rodney Scott made in August, in which he described the reservation’s southern
boundary as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on
the Southwest border” and a “remote desert that has facilitated decades of
drug loads, migrant deaths, and cartel activity.”

Regarding construction of a wall, Scott said, “Congress funded this work, a
Federal court has affirmed it, and CBP is carrying it out under the legal
authorities that apply. Under President Trump’s leadership, we are securing
the border and giving our agents the tools and support they need to protect
the American people.”

![A meme shows a light-skinned individual with a futuristic mask partially
covering their face. The words “Resistance is Futile” span the top of the
image in white block letters.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-05-at-8.07.29-AM.png?w=527)A post
on X from James Percival, general counsel of the Department of Homeland
Security, celebrates the denial of a request for an emergency injunction
against border wall construction filed by Tohono O’odham leadership in August.
Screenshot of X

With no sign the White House or the O’odham government is backing down, DHS
has cast off any pretense that the agency will work cooperatively with the
Nation. Within hours of the judge’s denial of the emergency injunction, on
Aug. 14, the department’s general counsel, James Percival, posted [a
celebratory meme](https://x.com/DHSGenCounsel/status/2088313210797441387)
depicting one of the cybernetic Star Trek supervillains known as “the Borg.”

“RESISTANCE IS FUTILE,” it read.

“We respect tribal sovereignty but not to the detriment of border security,”
he wrote. “This wall is getting built. Our authority is beyond dispute.”

* * *

The O’odham have inhabited the Sonoran Desert, from what is now Southern
Arizona to Mexico’s Sea of Cortez, for [thousands of
years](https://naair.arizona.edu/tohono-oodham-nation). According to the
tribe, roughly 14,000 of its 37,000 enrolled members live on tribal land west
of Tucson. Approximately 3,000 more reside in Mexico. At 2.8 million acres,
their reservation is the largest on the southern border by a long shot.

During President Donald Trump’s first term, Arizona saw 226 miles of border
wall built, but the Nation maintained its status as the longest unwalled
section in the state. Confirmation that things would be different this time
came in February, when CBP informed the tribe that it planned to seal off the
reservation entirely, tapping nearly [$52
billion](https://www.tucsonsentinel.com/local/report/021826_o-
odham_border_wall/tohono-oodham-warn-dhs-plans-build-wall-along-
tribes-62-mile-border-with-mexico/) from Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful
Bill Act.

![A dirt road passes through a lush Southwestern desert landscape. There is a
heavy metal fence on the left side of the frame and a jagged mountain
formation on the horizon.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/L1000719.jpg)A vehicle barrier marks the U.S. border
with Mexico in the Chukut Kuk District of the Tohono O’odham Nation. Cam
Mackey

The tribe’s elected leaders met with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in hopes
of changing the administration’s mind. As an enrolled citizen of the Cherokee
Nation, Mullin is the first Native American to head the department. “Maybe we
can work with this guy,” Jose recalled thinking.

But Mullin’s message was clear: We want to work with you, but we’re building
the wall. Justice Department attorneys were prepared to defend the project to
the Supreme Court. O’odham council member Vivian Juan-Saunders, who also
attended the April 21 meeting, recalls the secretary saying, “Don’t mess with
me.” Mullin’s office did not respond to questions from ProPublica, including
about the exchange.

The message was more direct the following month, when tribal leaders met with
Scott. According to Jose, the CBP commissioner told the delegation that if
they filed a lawsuit opposing the wall, the Nation could lose access to three
border gates members use to travel to and from Mexico. Accessible only to
tribal members, the gates are maintained at the discretion of CBP.

Juan-Saunders confirmed that CBP threatened to close the gates, as did another
council member, Jesse Navarro. CBP declined to comment on the alleged threat.

In June, a $1.3 billion contract to build the wall, known as the “Tucson 5”
project, was awarded to Sullivan Land Services Co., also known as SLS and
SLSCO. The Texas firm has a [long
history](https://www.texasobserver.org/biden-quietly-gave-border-wall-
contract-to-company-used-by-trump-abbott/) of Republican political donations
and was a [major recipient](https://www.texasobserver.org/colossal-waste-of-
money-texas-nears-1-billion-in-border-wall-contracts/) of border wall
contracts during Trump’s first term.

The O’odham filed [a lawsuit](https://www.tonation-nsn.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/001-Complaint-2026.06.16.pdf) to stop the project on
June 16 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. The tribe
contended it would reduce the size of its reservation, which can only be done
by Congress — and that the wall would mark an enduring act of trespass on
sovereign lands and destroy sacred cultural sites.

The administration’s plans cast aside decades of tribal cooperation with DHS,
the Nation’s lawyers argued, and came at a time of record-low border
crossings.

[Trump](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/q9mSItyjBzo) and his administration
have repeatedly claimed that the border is safer than ever, with CBP reporting
border apprehensions 94% lower than they were during the Biden presidency, and
Border Patrol “encounters” hitting their [lowest levels in more than 50
years](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/02/02/migrant-encounters-
at-the-us-mexico-border-are-at-their-lowest-level-in-more-than-50-years/). The
Nation underscored these figures as evidence that a wall is unnecessary.

The tribe’s interim chief of police, James Cook, claimed there had been a 90%
drop in reports of illegal entry over the preceding year, saying in a sworn
declaration that smuggling and other border-related crimes had “almost
disappeared.”

Benjamin S. Hollinder, a senior Border Patrol official, argued in a sworn
declaration opposing the tribe’s lawsuit that the absence of a wall on the
Nation has produced a funneling effect, channeling smugglers onto the
reservation, and saying that dynamic would intensify once the rest of Arizona
was walled off.

“Not having a border barrier system in this particular area makes it a
vulnerable and a desirable area for [transnational criminal organizations] to
operate,” wrote Hollinder. “If encounters of aliens entering illegally between
ports of entry increase, vulnerabilities in the area will become particularly
problematic.”

* * *

The Nation sought the preliminary injunction to bar border wall activity until
the litigation was resolved.

On the eve of a July 22 hearing, DHS [filed a
notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-07-21/pdf/2026-14604.pdf)
affirming that to accelerate the project, it was waiving, in whole or in part,
more than 30 laws, including several that mandate tribal consultation.

In court filings, the government acknowledged its long history of working
“cooperatively” with the tribal government while also arguing that the Nation
“does not hold veto power over the United States’ sovereign duty to secure its
borders.”

Trump administration attorneys contended that an injunction was premature;
planning was ongoing, thus problems the Nation envisioned could still be
addressed.

The government insisted construction would be limited to the Roosevelt
Reservation, a 60-foot-wide zone that runs across California, Arizona and New
Mexico on the U.S. side of the border, where CBP was authorized to construct
barriers as it saw fit.

Riyaz Kanji, the tribe’s lead attorney, argued the Roosevelt Reservation
doesn’t extend onto tribal land, and even if it did the rugged landscape would
force construction to diverge far from the 60-foot boundary.

Sweeping as its powers were, Kanji contended, DHS could not override a
sovereign government. The administration’s plans, he argued, constituted a
“blatant and unprecedented disregard for the tribe’s rights.”

Adam R.F. Gustafson, a Justice Department attorney, countered that the tribe
had already approved a barrier on its land many years ago. The question now
was what kind of barrier it should be. That was for DHS to decide, he argued.
The department was “committed” to consultation, he continued. “We take very
seriously the tribe’s views on this,” he told the court.

The judge appeared swayed by DHS’ assurances but needed time to consider. “I
don’t think the government is trying to go outside of that 60-foot strip,” he
said.

* * *

![A red and white sign in a desert landscape is seen through a barbed-wire
fence and warns against trespassing on the Tohono O’odham Nation for anyone
who’s not a tribal member.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/000000100003.jpg?w=2560)Signs placed by Tohono O’odham
tribal leaders warn contractors that their presence on the reservation would
be considered trespassing. Cam Mackey

The O’odham suspected the government would not be as mindful as it claimed.

Two days after the meeting with Mullin, the DHS secretary, a border wall
contractor had “inadvertently disturbed a cultural site” west of the
reservation. The crew had [bulldozed](https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-
environment/2026/04/30/border-wall-damage-indigenous-arizona/) a 70-foot swath
through the Las Playas Intaglio, a 200-foot long earthen etching in the shape
of a fish that was at least [6,500 years
old](https://mydigitalpublication.com/publication/?i=870459&p=30&view=issueViewer).
The site was well marked and well known to area archaeologists.

Wynona P. Larson Yazzie, an O’odham tribal elder, Marine Corps veteran and
former tribal police officer, had organized prayer runs that included stops at
the intaglio. She’d visited the site the day before its destruction. Since
then, she’d closely followed the Nation’s lawsuit.

On Aug. 6, Larson Yazzie saw a disturbing filing from the tribe’s attorneys.
They’d received word that in four days government contractors would enter the
reservation to conduct tests. DHS, the tribe argued, was “exploiting” the
judge’s reflection period to “move forward with highly disputed actions.”

Tribal leaders erected dozens of 8-foot-wide “no trespassing” signs along the
three main access roads leading through the reservation to the border.

Larson Yazzie, meanwhile, began making plans of her own.

She was joined by Amy Juan, a longtime O’odham activist. Juan, 40, had grown
up riding in her grandfather’s truck over the clanking cattle guard at Ko:li
Ki:jig, a traditional crossing on the U.S.-Mexico line. After 9/11, a locking
gate was placed over the cattle guard. The Border Patrol built a “forward
operating base” near her grandparents’ home that would eventually feature a
helipad, a detention space and an endless cycle of agents. Around the
reservation’s perimeter, CBP established some of the largest Border Patrol
stations in the country. Checkpoints went up on roads leading north.

![Two people visit across a fence made of barbed wire strung between thick
metal posts in a desert landscape. In the background, a surveillance camera
rises above them.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5855.jpg?w=2560)O’odham tribal members Daniel
Oriol Figueroa Cervantes, left, from Mexico, and Amy Juan, from Arizona, visit
over the border barrier at the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on Aug. 29. Ryan
Devereaux/ProPublica

Human rights groups
[documented](https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/amr51/018/2012/en/)
U.S.-born tribal members being arrested and deported, and verbal and physical
abuse by Border Patrol agents. CBP did not respond when asked about the
report’s allegations.

For Juan, the Nation’s collaboration with DHS had sacrificed safety and civil
liberties for elusive gains. Virtually everyone on the reservation had been
touched by the dark side of border smuggling. During the mid-2000s, some
tribal members, enticed by a chance at life-changing money, got involved in
moving people and drugs, fueling cycles of arrest and incarceration that
exacerbated challenges the community was already facing.

At the same time, virtually everyone also had a story about negative
interactions with the Border Patrol — a child traumatized at a checkpoint, an
unlawful traffic stop or a loved one assaulted by an agent.

“We want safety and the same respect as the next person,” Juan said. “We’ve
never been against keeping people safe, but at what cost?”

Larson Yazzie was similarly concerned. She worried that in the face of DHS
pressure the Nation would fold and, like the intaglio, the borderlands would
be lost.

* * *

![An Indigenous person stands near a burning fire surrounded by camping chairs
in a desert landscape campsite.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/L1000668.jpg)A tribal member stands near the fire
burning in the Tadai Me:i prayer camp in early September. Cam Mackey

Prayer fires are an important O’odham tradition, often convened in moments of
communal struggle. To Larson Yazzie, the coming of a wall was such a time.

The chosen site was symbolic: the border gate at Ko:li Ki:jig. The camp had
limited amenities — cots and chairs that encircled the fire, a cooler for ice,
a weathered canopy for relief from the sun. They called it Tadai Me:i —
roadrunner on fire.

Someone was always awake to watch the flame, which was lit on Aug. 9, as the
Trump administration’s contractors were preparing to enter the reservation.
The first drone sighting in the area was recorded the following night, at
11:43 p.m., documented in the first of two activity logs. Kept in spiral
notebooks, the logs offered a minute-by-minute account of what participants in
the ceremony saw and heard.

The handwritten observations, shared with ProPublica, span 13 days and chart a
steady escalation by DHS, culminating in an elite tactical team that blocked
tribal authorities from issuing trespassing citations to contractors or
removing them.

The camp wasn’t a protest site like those seen in Minneapolis, Chicago or
other cities over the past year. Participants didn’t shout at passing Border
Patrol agents. They focused on the fire, making sure there was enough sugai —
creosote bush, a fragrant desert plant — to keep it burning. They were in
ceremony, concentrating on morning prayers and nightly cleanses. The
atmosphere was that of a family gathering in a moment of crisis. There were
jokes and levity amid the uncertainty.

Larson Yazzie knew at least one legislative council member who opposed the
gathering. They feared it could lead to large groups converging on the
reservation to physically block the border wall, in an occupation similar to
the 10-month protest on Standing Rock Sioux land that halted construction of
the Dakota Access Pipeline in 2016. The idea terrified tribal leaders. With
its lethal heat and unforgiving terrain, the desert was dangerous enough
without outsiders squaring off against Border Patrol.

A ceremonial fire burns on Aug. 27 at a prayer camp near the traditional Ko:li
Ki:jig border crossing on the Tohono O’odham Nation. Nate Sosa

Supporters of the ceremonial fire were themselves uneasy. They knew the story
of [Ray Mattia](https://theintercept.com/2023/06/26/border-patrol-killing-
raymond-mattia/), the 58-year-old who was shot and killed by the Border Patrol
in 2023 while unarmed on the doorstep of his home on the reservation. Agents,
who were backing tribal police on the call,
[claimed](https://www.courthousenews.com/border-patrol-agents-seek-qualified-
immunity-for-killing-unarmed-native-american/?ref=lookoutnews.org) to have
mistaken a cellphone he was holding for a gun.

“My fear is that they gonna start shooting us,” said 24-year-old camp visitor
Collin Quasule. Quasule had videos on his phone of recent interactions he’d
had with federal agents, including agents trailing him as he drove around the
reservation, following him to his home, pulling him over without explaining
why, refusing to accept his legal name and birthdate, and winking at him when
he protested his detention.

Across the reservation, community members were on the lookout for large trucks
traveling together with out-of-state plates. On Aug. 12, Juan received a call
about a caravan: six trucks with Texas plates, following an unmarked SUV with
government plates. She called the tribe’s police department. The caravan was
intercepted and escorted off the land by tribal authorities. The driver of the
unmarked vehicle was confirmed to be a Border Patrol agent. The interception
was one of nearly a dozen tribal police recorded over a three-day period.

During the camp’s first seven days, the activity log filled with nearly 665
observations, mostly federal agents buzzing around their location.

![A lined white notebook page containing log entries tracking Border Patrol
movements and surveillance sits on a table.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5803.jpg?w=1149)An activity log kept by tribal
members documents border wall construction and law enforcement activity on the
Tohono O’odham Nation. Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica

While many would drive by without stopping, other agents would park and watch.
At least one was reported snapping photos of the campers. ProPublica later
obtained video of an agent doing exactly that. Mexican security forces, both
military and police, were also observed conversing with Border Patrol agents
over the international boundary. “It appeared that the 2 BPs were showing the
Mexicans pictures on their phones,” read an Aug. 11 entry.

“Surveillance has heightened,” Juan said, days after the prayer fire was lit.
“Drones, helicopters, a lot of air activity.” The choppers included both
marked CBP and what appeared to be military Black Hawks. The drones were of
the handheld quadcopter variety, let loose directly over the camp, at times
during prayer song ceremonies.

On the fourth night, a gathering was held. Upwards of 100 people turned up,
including members of distant sister tribes.

The evening was peaceful until Juan received a text from an elder couple who’d
left early to return to their home near Tucson. The Border Patrol had stopped
them at a checkpoint a half-mile outside the reservation, they reported. The
officers said they were conducting an “immigration check” and asked to see
tribal ID.

“Where you guys coming from?” the agent asked.

“Ceremony,” the couple replied.

“Oh,” the agent said, “is that the one going on down south?”

The encounter was unusual, said Juan. The checkpoint is rarely staffed. When
agents are on hand, she said, “they never ask us for a tribal ID.”

When Juan shared the information with the gathering, people immediately began
packing up, afraid, she surmised, of a late-night encounter with Border
Patrol.

A Border Patrol agent stops to film the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on Sept. 30.
Davy Cross

On Aug. 14, Judge Richard J. Leon declined the Nation’s injunction request. “I
fully expect the government in the months ahead to follow through on its
guarantees of consultation and cooperation with the Nation to address the
Nation’s concerns regarding border wall construction!” he wrote.

Eleven days later, on Aug. 25, the Border Patrol sent the Nation its one-
minute notice that the contractors were coming. Larson Yazzie jumped in her
truck and raced for the border to document what was happening. An agent on
foot stopped her. He’d laid a spike strip in the road ahead, he warned. Larson
Yazzie filmed the contractors in the distance.

When the tribal police department’s interim chief arrived, he too was stopped
at a Border Patrol roadblock. A trio of Border Patrol supervisors approached,
including two from a nearby station and a third representing BORTAC, the
agency’s special operations wing. The SWAT-style agents wore desert camo,
masks and patterned scarves favored by U.S. military units in Iraq and
Afghanistan.

It was only after promising not to interfere that the tribal police chief was
permitted to record. He observed three drilling rigs manned by a handful of
operators. An equal number of agents stood guard. The contractors’ heavy
vehicles were all beyond the 60-foot zone that government attorneys assured
the judge they would not leave.

The chief also encountered a trio of Bureau of Indian Affairs agents, who
claimed to have been sent on orders from Washington, D.C. Their mission, they
said, was to “preserve the peace and monitor activities.”

* * *

![On the left, a red and yellow painted sign with graffiti-style white letters
warns that “Community Members Only!” are allowed on the Tohono O’odham Nation.
A white and green Border Patrol truck is driving on a dirt road on the
right.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/000000110008.jpg)A Border Patrol vehicle is parked
near the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on the Tohono O’odham Nation. Cam Mackey

For the prayer camp’s participants, the need to relight the flame, which they
had extinguished after a seven-day ceremony, was self-evident. They began that
night.

Davy Cross, a stocky 57-year-old with an intricate tattoo running down the
left side of his face, was tending the fire when, at 4:33 a.m., he noticed
buzzing above his head.

At first, the machines were visible. There were at least five. “I seen all the
red lights,” Cross recalled. But as they got lower, the drones went dark.
Cross could still hear them and feel the draft of the rotors against his skin.
Then, he said, “they disappeared.”

The drones were soon replaced by an airplane and a helicopter. Shortly after 9
a.m., a caravan of Border Patrol and construction vehicles trundled into view.
The work trucks continued on, but much of the Border Patrol force remained,
forming a semicircle around the camp with Mexican state police closing the
loop on the other side of the line.

“We got surround[ed] by over 30 vehicles,” Cross wrote in the activity log. A
[video of the
moment](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DcmMIgThmmI/?stkn=MXduZ3pmOWNvNWU4bg%3D%3D)
spread across social media in the borderlands.

The tribe’s attorneys filed an appeal of the judge’s order allowing
construction to proceed and pleaded for a halt to the government’s activities.
They argued that the Trump administration was making “a mockery” of the
court’s expectation of “consultation and cooperation.”

A convoy of Border Patrol and construction vehicles pass the Tadai Me:i prayer
camp on Aug. 29. Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica

That night at the camp, Larson Yazzie was singing prayer songs when Juan
pulled in. It was near midnight. Border Patrol agents were coming and going
constantly. Some passed without stopping. Others idled at the edge of the
firelight while the red lights of a surveillance blimp blinked over the
mountains to the east.

Tadai Me:i wasn’t the only pocket of resistance on the border. In Texas, the
Trump administration’s plans to run a wall through Big Bend National Park had
brought together an unusual coalition that saw [environmental
nonprofits](https://biologicaldiversity.org/w/news/press-releases/emergency-
injunction-sought-to-block-big-bend-border-construction-despite-government-
pause-2026-08-17/?_gl=1*4p9amg*_gcl_au*MzY4NDMyOTg3LjE3ODI4NDUxMDQ.) and
[river guides](https://americancanoe.org/paddlers-in-texas-speak-up-about-the-
impacts-of-the-proposed-wall-in-big-bend/) standing with
[hunters](https://www.backcountryhunters.org/news/details/texas-bha-raises-
serious-concerns-with-big-bend-border-wall),
[ranchers](https://apnews.com/article/border-wall-lawsuit-texas-trump-
immigration-3c080168e2d0c5a053263c91a52b923c) and [local
sheriffs](https://www.hstoday.us/subject-matter-areas/border-security/5-west-
texas-sheriffs-oppose-big-bend-border-wall-construction/) in opposition to the
project. One week before the armed convoy rolled onto the Tohono O’odham
reservation, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott announced that after speaking with
the secretary of DHS, he’d secured a pause on the controversial project.

“There are technology tools that don’t include barriers,” [the governor
said](https://www.kwtx.com/2026/08/17/gov-abbott-says-homeland-security-
assured-him-there-will-be-no-construction-any-type-barrier-big-bend/) at a
press conference. “Think of drones, think of fiber optics.”

Last week, a judge [granted](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/judge-
bars-building-texas-mexico-border-barrier-big-bend-national-park-2026-10-03/)
a preliminary injunction halting construction in the Big Bend area while a
lawsuit against the project proceeds.

To Juan, it was darkly ironic. For two and a half decades, the Nation had been
a laboratory for the technology Abbott described. Yet when tribal leaders made
that case, they were told to stand down; the wall was coming whether they
accepted it or not. “What makes Texas the exception to us is very clear,” Juan
said. “It’s good old boy conversations that are happening between the
politicians and the CBP commissioners and Markwayne Mullin.”

while a ceremonial fire burns in the
foreground.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-

The early fire watch that morning fell to a young Pascua Yaqui member named
Nate Sosa.

At 3:28 a.m., Sosa heard a noise — a round being chambered in a weapon. A
Border Patrol agent had exited his vehicle. With a long gun slung low across
his back, he shined a light into Mexico. He then walked within feet of the
campers asleep on their cots.

A half an hour later, a drone flew in from the north, followed by a
helicopter. After that came a convoy dozens of vehicles long. At 6:02, while
Larson Yazzie was leading the camp in prayer, a helicopter passed overhead. An
hour later, a drone ascended above the fire.

Liz Quiroga, a 28-year-old tribal member and regular at the prayer site, sat
with the camp’s logbook open in her lap. Over the next five days, the book
would fill with 379 observations. Nearly two-thirds involved Border Patrol
units near the fire. The arrival of Mexican authorities was documented six
times. An additional 39 entries referenced unmarked vehicles and suspected
“undercovers.” Whether those individuals were Border Patrol, contractors or
tribal police was unclear. The logbook cataloged a dozen instances of aircraft
flying over the camp, including four helicopters, three planes and five
drones.

“Nobody has any idea what’s actually happening out here,” Quiroga said. “This
is true dystopia.”

While its legal challenge continues, the Nation has ceased attempting to
remove border wall contractors from its lands.

The camp and the surveillance that’s come with it remain.
